name: Reading Central Bank Communication
title: Reading Central Bank Communication
answer: This page covers the use of natural language processing and machine learning to read central bank communication, including policy statements, meeting minutes, speeches, and press conference transcripts. The aim is to extract measurable signals about the policy stance, forward guidance, uncertainty, and the balance of risks. Work in this area sits within macroeconomic econometrics and treats text as an input to models of inflation, output, and asset prices. The page is part of The AI Economist and assumes a reader who follows monetary policy but is not a machine learning engineer.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the use of natural language processing and machine learning to read central bank communication, including policy statements, meeting minutes, speeches, and press conference transcripts. The aim is to extract measurable signals about the policy stance, forward guidance, uncertainty, and the balance of risks. Work in this area sits within macroeconomic econometrics and treats text as an input to models of inflation, output, and asset prices. The page is part of The AI Economist and assumes a reader who follows monetary policy but is not a machine learning engineer.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on text corpora gathered from central bank websites, official archives, and transcript services, usually stored in structured databases with timestamps and speaker metadata. A typical pipeline includes scraping or API access, cleaning, sentence splitting, and tokenization before any model is applied. Computation ranges from simple lexicon lookups on a laptop to transformer-based language models that require GPU or cloud instances. Versioned datasets and model artifacts are common so that results can be reproduced when a central bank revises or republishes a document.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts convert text into numerical features using dictionary-based scores for hawkish and dovish language, topic models, word embeddings, or fine-tuned classifiers trained on labeled policy stances. These features are then used in event studies, regressions, or nowcasting models that link changes in communication to yields, exchange rates, or inflation expectations. A common workflow is to compare the tone of a new statement with the previous one and with market expectations, then test whether the residual tone predicts the immediate market reaction. Human judgment remains part of the loop because central bank language is deliberately ambiguous and context dependent.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Central bank texts are generally public but may be subject to terms of use, copyright, or restrictions on bulk downloading, so provenance and access records matter. Model risk is high because a small change in wording can carry a large policy signal, and an automated reading can overstate or miss that signal. Reproducibility requires documenting the corpus version, preprocessing choices, and model parameters, especially when a central bank edits or reissues a document. Interpretability is also a concern, since a black-box sentiment score is less useful to a policy analyst than a score that can be traced back to specific phrases. Nothing on this page is legal or investment advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of work is toward real-time parsing of press conferences and statements, with outputs available within minutes of release rather than hours or days. Multilingual models are becoming more common as analysts compare communication across the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan, and other institutions in their own languages. Researchers are also working on models that separate deliberate forward guidance from incidental tone, and on linking text measures more tightly to high-frequency market data. Over time, the field is likely to move from static sentiment scores to structured summaries of policy reaction functions and risk assessments.
